newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Argos ups profit, reassures investors.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Argos ups profit, reassures investors.

text.p: British retailer Argos Plc reported a 14 percent increase in annual profits on Monday and set out to reassure investors that a Christmas sales upset, which rocked its shares, was just a temporary setback.

Argos, operator of more than 400 catalogue showrooms across Britain, posted pretax profits of 141.4 million pounds ($226.3 million) in the year to December 28 1996, up from 124.4 million in the previous 12 months. Sales rose 15.6 percent to 1.66 billion pounds from 1.44 billion.
Earnings per share were up 18.2 percent to 32.5 pence, and the dividend was increased by 23.1 percent to 16 pence a share.
But the group was not optimistic about retail spending overall for 1997, saying its research showed that the 1996 upturn seemed to have faded.

"Our research does tell us though that consumer confidence is off the peak that it was in 1996," Finance Director Bob Stewart said, adding that it was uncertain whether this would remain the trend for the rest of 1997.

This cautious outlook pushed Argos shares down on Monday morning to the day's low of 628 pence per share, down 11 pence on the day. But by 1240 GMT, they had recovered to 647p after the company's reassurances.
As the group warned in January, sales in the final three months, including Christmas were slower than expected.
The group blamed weakness in three of its key markets -- toys, small electrical goods and jewellery -- for the slowdown.
The unexpected sales hiccup forced the top rated retailer to admit in January that second half sales had been lower than expected.
The profit warning stunned investors who had been hoping for a bumper Christmas from one of Britain's retail sector leaders.

Argos's shares plummeted to a 1997 low of 598p and although they have bounced back, the firm will later this month leave Britain's FTSE-100 Index of blue chip stocks because it has dropped down the ranks in terms of market capitalisation.

Stewart said in the final quarter of the year toys, small electricals and jewellery, which together accounted for around 50 percent of sales, achieved just two percent growth in like for like sales, compared to eight percent for the group's other products.
"We've done quite a detailed inquest on the final quarter 1996 and there were one or two minor things that we got wrong - but the overriding feature was those three markets."

Stewart said in an interview that despite slower sales the group had managed to achieve "quite significant" market share improvements in toys and small electricals in the final quarter, and at least held on to market share in jewellery. And since Christmas sales in all three categories had picked up again.
Argos also warned that higher costs in the first half of 1997 would make it tough to beat last year's first half result when profits surged more than 50 percent.
The group continued to throw off cash, ending the year with about 100 million pounds. Last year Argos handed shareholders 127 million pounds via a special dividend.

This year the group plans to open 41 new stores, making a total of 435 by the year end, including closures. And it is on course to open five pilot shops in the Netherlands by the end of February 1998.
Stewart said the group would continue to test out its no-frills First Stop experiment, which offers shoppers a limited range of goods at cheap prices. There are currently three stores trading.
